intro: The SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam was held on 28 October 2026 in three shifts. Based on the reported summaries, Shifts 1 and 2 were described as moderate to difficult, while Shift 3 was perceived as easy to moderate. Reported good‑attempt ranges for most sections fall between 14 and 25 questions, though these figures are unofficial and SSC normalises scores across shifts. Shift 3 has only a limited review, so its data should be treated as provisional.

faqs.q: What was the overall difficulty level reported for the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam on 28 October 2026?
faqs.a: According to the shift summaries, Shifts 1 and 2 were described as moderate to difficult (with some variation), while Shift 3 was reported as easy to moderate. The overall perception therefore spans from easy‑moderate to moderate‑difficult across the three shifts.

faqs.q: How did candidates perform in the Reasoning section on 28 October 2026?
faqs.a: In Shift 1, Reasoning was noted as the easiest section with 18–23 questions attempted well. Shift 2 described Reasoning as moderate with 18–25 good attempts. Shift 3, despite limited data, mentioned lengthy statements that increased time pressure but did not provide reliable good‑attempt numbers.

faqs.q: What are the unofficial good‑attempt ranges for General Awareness and Quantitative Aptitude on 28 October 2026?
faqs.a: For Shift 1, General Awareness had about 14–18 good attempts and Quantitative Aptitude 13–20. For Shift 2, General Awareness ranged 12–24 and Quantitative Aptitude 14–23. These numbers are unofficial and subject to SSC’s cross‑shift normalisation.

faqs.q: Is a complete analysis available for all shifts of the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam on 28 October 2026?
faqs.a: Shifts 1 and 2 have reported summaries, but Shift 3 is only partially reviewed; the partial analysis is limited and requires further corroboration before being considered comprehensive.

faqs.q: How does SSC normalise scores across the shifts for the SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 exam on 28 October 2026?
faqs.a: SSC applies a standard normalisation process that adjusts raw scores from each shift to a common scale, ensuring that candidates are compared fairly regardless of the shift they attended. This means the unofficial good‑attempt figures should be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive.
